prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows an indoor booth or counter enclosure in the foreground (0.3 to 1.5 metres away) with a very bright vertical partition pillar ~0.3 to 0.5 metres in front of the camera wearer that shifts from the centre-left in frames 1–2 to the right edge in frames 3–5 as the wearer steps left and approaches the counter. A masked person stands on the right behind the counter at roughly 1.0 to 1.3 metres away, alongside a monitor, sanitizer bottle, and keyboard on the lower-left counter (~0.7 to 1.2 metres away, separated from the person by ~0.4 metres) that all come within arm's reach of both the person and the camera wearer by frames 4–5. The person faces forward and slightly left, looking down at the counter in frame 1, left in frame 2, and directly toward the camera wearer in frames 3–5, while the vertical frame partially occludes the counter in frames 1–2 and heavily occludes the right side of the person's body in frame 3. Compared to the RGB strip, where bright outdoor sunlight and reflections through the glass doors complicate distance perception, the depth map clearly separates the near vertical pillar and foreground shelving on the right from the mid-ground person and counter equipment. However, the depth map is unreliable on the transparent glass entrance doors in the background (~2.5 to 4 metres behind the person), rendering them pitch black as infinite depth while treating the surrounding transparent glass panes as solid opaque surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates the foreground objects inside the booth across the five frames, showing the person on the right (~1.0 to 1.3 metres from the camera wearer) positioned ~0.3 to 0.5 metres to the right of a counter setup on the lower left (~0.7 to 1.2 metres away) where a monitor sit above a keyboard and a sanitizer bottle. Across the sequence, as the camera wearer moves left and closer to the counter, the person turns their head from facing down and left in frames 1–2 to facing and looking directly toward the camera wearer in frames 3–5, while extending their right hand onto the keyboard (within arm's reach of both the person and the wearer) and keeping their left hand near the blue plastic bags on the lower right. The person's lower body below the hips is out of view behind the counter in all frames, and in frame 3 the foreground partition pillar occludes the right half of their torso and head. This map makes it easier than the RGB alone to track the exact contour overlap between the person's reaching right arm and the keyboard in frames 4–5, as well as the distinct boundaries of the bottle and monitor against the cluttered counter. However, the segmentation is unreliable in several places: it splits the partially occluded person into two overlapping masks in frame 3, misclassifies the bottle as a remote in frame 1 and the monitor as a tv (frames 1–3) or laptop (frames 4–5), fails to detect the keyboard in frames 1 and 3 or the foreground blue bags entirely, and mislabels a blue outdoor bin ~2.5 metres behind the person as a chair (frame 2), person (frame 4), and car (frame 5).
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks the upper-body and facial keypoints of the single person standing on the right (~1.0 to 1.3 metres in front of the camera wearer) behind the counter, while all scene furniture and background structures (~0.3 to 4 metres away) remain unrendered on the black canvas. The eye, nose, and ear keypoints show the person's head tilted down in frame 1, turned in profile to the left in frame 2, occluded on the right side in frame 3, and facing directly toward the camera wearer in frames 4–5 as the wearer moves left and closer, causing the skeleton to shift upward and expand in the frame. The arm keypoints show both hands down near the counter and blue bags (within the person's arm's reach) in frames 1–2, before the right wrist extends ~0.4 metres to the left to rest on the counter keyboard in frames 4–5 (bringing the hand within arm's reach of the camera wearer) while the left wrist stays down on the right. The skeleton ends at the hip keypoints because the legs are occluded below the counter edge, and in frame 3 the foreground vertical pillar occludes the left shoulder and left arm. Compared to the RGB image, where dim interior lighting and glare obscure joint positions, the pose map clearly reveals the torso orientation and bilateral shoulder-to-wrist geometry, though it is unreliable in frame 2 (missing left wrist/hand keypoints), frame 3 (collapsing the torso into a narrow sliver under pillar occlusion), and frame 4 (disconnecting the right wrist keypoint from the right elbow and misplacing the left arm joints).
